_note: Flight School v3 (docs/LEARNING_DESIGN.md §5): 6 lessons and a check ride, in map order (each lesson's `place` is its Moon-map pin). Authored in tools/build_course.py. Every fact cites a {title,url} and names the repo data file(s) it comes from (`from`, relative to backend/data); tests check every number in a fact appears in those files (or is recomputed, for `calc`). Steps accept voice or taps; app/academy/grade.py lists the accept types.
title: Junior Astronaut Academy

lessons.title: Know your Moon
lessons.brief: The Moon always shows Earth the same face. Let's explore both sides.

facts.text: Artemis II flew its crew around the Moon in April 2026. NASA plans the first south-pole landing for Artemis IV, targeted for 2028.
NASA's 2024 list of 9 possible landing regions near the south pole includes Malapert Massif and de Gerlache Rim 2.

source.title: NASA Provides Update on Artemis III Moon Landing Regions (Oct 2024)

facts.text: The Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us.
Shackleton is a crater about 21 km wide and about 4 km deep. The south pole is on its edge.

source.title: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Shackleton

facts.text: Craters that never see the Sun are some of the coldest places measured, near -235 C.

source.title: Paige et al. 2010, Diviner observations of cold traps, Science 330

steps.prompt: Apollo 11 landed on a dark patch, the Sea of Tranquility. Find it.
steps.do: Tap it on the Moon, or say its name
steps.hint: It's the dark patch right of the middle.
steps.success: Copy. The Sea of Tranquility, July 1969.

steps.prompt: Standing there, could you see Earth in the sky?
steps.hint: This side of the Moon always faces Earth.
steps.success: Yes. Earth hangs in the same spot there.

steps.prompt: Do people on Earth ever see the Moon's far side?
steps.reveal: Never. The Moon turns once per trip around Earth.
steps.hint: Guess first. Then we'll see.
steps.success: Right. The Moon turns once per trip around Earth.

steps.prompt: Turn the Moon to show the far side.
steps.hint: Tap Far, or drag the Moon around.
steps.success: Roger. The far side gets sunlight too.

steps.prompt: Now find the south pole. It's inside the gold ring.
steps.hint: Tap inside the gold ring.
steps.success: Roger. Shackleton crater. Our outpost goes here.

lessons.title: Lessons from Apollo
lessons.brief: Every mission teaches the next. Follow the crews from Apollo to Artemis.

facts.text: Surveyor 3 sent 6,326 pictures. In 1969 Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and took about 10 kg of parts home, including its TV camera.
John Young and Charlie Duke drove the Apollo 16 rover 26.7 km across the Moon's highlands.
Artemis II passed Apollo 13's record of 248,655 miles from Earth on April 6, 2026.

source.title: NASA: Artemis II crew eclipses record for farthest human spaceflight

facts.text: The Artemis II crew proposed the names Integrity and Carroll for two craters. They are not approved yet.

source.title: NASA: Artemis II crew eclipses record for farthest human spaceflight

steps.prompt: Apollo 11 landed on a mare. What does mare mean?
steps.hint: Look at the dark patch on the Moon.
steps.success: Yes. A mare is a plain of old lava.

steps.prompt: Robot Surveyor 3 took photos here. Apollo 12 took one part home. Which?
steps.hint: It took photos. What takes photos?
steps.success: Correct. Scientists studied what the Moon did to it.

steps.prompt: Apollo 13 went farther from Earth than anyone. Did Artemis II beat it?
steps.reveal: Artemis II passed it on April 6, 2026.
steps.hint: Guess first. Then hear Houston.
steps.success: Yes. Artemis II passed it on April 6, 2026.

steps.prompt: Artemis II's crew picked a crater name: Integrity. Tap Orientale, then Ohm.
steps.do: Tap the glowing places in order: 1, then 2
steps.hint: Orientale is the big bullseye. Ohm is above it.
steps.success: Roger. Integrity sits halfway. Name not official yet.

steps.prompt: Listen to Charlie Duke. Who landed on the Moon with him?
steps.do: Tap Hear Charlie Duke, then pick a name
steps.hint: Tap Hear Charlie Duke. He says the name first.
steps.success: Correct. John Young. They drove 26.7 km.

lessons.title: Talk on the radio
lessons.brief: Radio is noisy, so crews keep it short. Copy means I heard you.

facts.text: Artemis II and Houston really say it: "Houston, we have you loud and clear." ... "Houston copies all."

source.title: NASA Artemis II audio: Houston, We Have You Loud and Clear

facts.text: The Moon is about 384,400 km away, so a radio call takes about 1.3 seconds each way.
In our model of April 2026, Earth was up 93% of the time at Malapert and 45% at Shackleton Rim.

steps.prompt: What does "copy" mean on the radio?
steps.do: Tap an answer, or say it
steps.hint: Copy is about hearing.
steps.success: Roger. Copy means I heard you.

steps.prompt: CAPCOM: "Commander, set the heaters to 40 percent." Say it back.
steps.capcom: Commander, set the heaters to 40 percent.
steps.do: Repeat the order out loud, or type it
steps.hint: Say what to set, and how much.
steps.success: Good readback. Heaters to 40.

steps.prompt: How long does your voice take to reach Earth?
steps.reveal: About 1.3 seconds. Radio moves at light speed.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. About 1.3 seconds, at light speed.

steps.prompt: Earth hangs over the Moon's near side. Which outpost sees Earth more?
steps.hint: Malapert sits on the side facing Earth.
steps.success: Malapert. Earth was up 9.5 of 10 days.

steps.prompt: Static! You missed the last order. Ask CAPCOM to repeat it, radio style.
steps.do: Say it out loud, or type it
steps.hint: Radio talk for repeat: two words, ending in again.
steps.success: Copy. Say again asks for a repeat.

lessons.title: Power from the Sun
lessons.brief: Solar panels need sunlight. At the south pole, the Sun skims the horizon.

facts.text: Day and night sweep around the Moon once every 29.5 Earth days.
At the pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5 degrees above a flat horizon.
Averaged over a year, Shackleton's rim gets sunlight about 86% of the time and Malapert about 73%.

source.title: Glaser et al. 2018, Illumination conditions at the lunar poles, Planetary and Space Science

facts.text: In our model of April 2026, Malapert was in sunlight 35% of the time.
Its longest dark spell in that window lasted 157 hours, more than 6 days.

steps.prompt: Tap the line where day meets night.
steps.hint: Where the bright part turns dark.
steps.success: That's the terminator. It sweeps around monthly.
steps.fail: Not quite. Find the shadow's edge.

steps.prompt: At the south pole, how high does the Sun climb?
steps.reveal: It skims the horizon, never more than about 1.5 degrees up.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. It skims the horizon all day.

steps.prompt: Which site stays sunny for our 10-day mission?
steps.hint: Malapert goes dark early in our mission.
steps.success: Shackleton Rim. Sun all 10 days in our model.

steps.prompt: Night is coming at Malapert. Move power to the heaters so the pipes don't freeze.
steps.hint: The heaters need more power. Tap Heaters up.
steps.success: Copy. That dark spell lasted 157 hours.

lessons.title: Radiation and storms
lessons.brief: The Sun sometimes throws out fast particles. On the Moon, nothing stops them.

facts.text: China's Chang'e 4 lander measured 1369 microsieverts a day on the Moon, about 2.6 times the cosmic-ray dose inside the ISS, 523 microsieverts a day.

source.title: Zhang et al. 2020, First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface, Science Advances 6:eaaz1334

facts.text: In May 2024 a real solar particle storm hit space near Earth and the Moon. Earth also got huge auroras.
After a big flare, particles can arrive in tens of minutes to a few hours.
On Orion, a sensor gives up to 1 hour of warning. The crew hides behind packed bags for up to 24 hours.
Game doses are doubled so storms matter in 10 days. The powered shields are pretend tech.

source.title: Outpost Luna radiation data and game assumptions

steps.prompt: Earth has a magnetic shield and thick air. Does the Moon?
steps.reveal: No. Fast particles reach the Moon's ground.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. Fast particles reach the Moon's ground.

steps.prompt: Houston: particles likely within an hour. When do you shelter?
steps.hint: Particles move fast. An hour is short. Act early.
steps.success: Right. Get ready before the storm hits.

steps.prompt: Alert! A solar particle storm, like the real one in May 2024. Your order?
steps.hint: Get the crew under cover. Tap Into the shelter.
steps.success: Copy. Crew in the shelter. Dose rate way down.

steps.prompt: Doctors count radiation in mSv. So what is an mSv?
steps.hint: It measures how much radiation you got.
steps.success: Correct. One mSv is about 10 chest x-rays.

lessons.title: Air, water and ice
lessons.brief: Water is heavy to launch. Ice on the Moon could become water and air.

facts.text: In 2009 NASA crashed a Centaur rocket stage, about 2,300 kg, into Cabeus crater near the south pole.

source.title: Colaprete et al. 2010, Detection of water in the LCROSS ejecta plume, Science 330

facts.text: The plume held about 155 kg of water, about 5.6% of the soil by mass.

source.title: Colaprete et al. 2010, Detection of water in the LCROSS ejecta plume, Science 330

facts.text: Shackleton Rim is about 10 km from the middle of Shackleton crater; Malapert is about 130 km away.

source.title: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Shackleton

steps.prompt: Why would NASA crash a rocket into a dark crater?
steps.reveal: To dig up buried stuff. LCROSS found about 155 kg of water.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. Water hid in regolith, the Moon's dust.

steps.prompt: The LCROSS rocket hit Cabeus crater, near the south pole. Find it.
steps.do: Tap it on the Moon, or say its name
steps.hint: It's close to the south pole, in the middle.
steps.success: Roger. Cabeus crater, 2009.

steps.prompt: Ice hides in Shackleton crater. Which outpost is closer to it?
steps.hint: Look at the Moon. The rim sits right on the crater.
steps.success: The rim, about 10 km. Malapert, about 129.

steps.prompt: Life support is getting low. Send the rover for ice!
steps.hint: The rover can dig up ice. Tap Rover: get ice.
steps.success: Copy. Rover rolling out for ice.

steps.prompt: Fill the blank: "Ice hides in the Moon's dusty soil, the ____."

accept.sentence: Ice hides in the Moon's dusty soil, the ____.

steps.do: Tap the missing word, or say it
steps.hint: The word for Moon dust starts with r.
steps.success: Right. Regolith, the Moon's dusty soil.

lessons.title: Check ride
lessons.brief: Your check ride: two days at Shackleton Rim. A real particle storm is coming.

facts.text: The storm in this ride is based on the real solar particle storm of 2024-05-09. Earth also got huge auroras.
The ride starts when Earth is above Shackleton Rim's horizon in our April 2026 model, so the radio works.

steps.prompt: Earth is up over the rim. Can you call Houston now?
steps.reveal: Yes. Earth is up, so the radio works.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. Earth is up, so the radio works.

steps.prompt: Ask Houston about space weather.
steps.hint: Say: Houston, any space weather?
steps.success: Copy. Houston sees an active region. Stay sharp.

steps.prompt: Solar particle storm! Based on the real May 2024 storm. Your order?
steps.hint: Get the whole crew under cover.
steps.success: Copy. Crew in the shelter.

steps.prompt: The storm has passed. Bring the crew out of the shelter.
steps.hint: The crew can leave the shelter now.
steps.success: Copy. Crew is out. Back to work.

steps.prompt: Life support is dropping. Send the rover for ice before day 2 ends.
steps.hint: The rover can dig up ice.
steps.success: Copy. Rover rolling out for ice.
steps.fail: Negative. The rover needs to fetch ice.
